body.text: Long-term human resilience often comes down to biological mechanisms like Campylobacter jejuni. Clinical evidence shows how small cellular and systemic shifts compound into measurable health outcomes.

Campylobacter jejuni is a Gram-negative, helical-shaped, motile, microaerophilic, pathogenic bacterium in the genus Campylobacter. It commonly colonizes the intestinal tracts of poultry and other animals and is a major cause of bacterial gastroenteritis in humans worldwide.

jejuni has several characteristics that contribute to its ability to survive and colonize its hosts. Its flagella provide motility though intestinal mucus, while adhesion, invasion, and other virulence mechanisms allow the bacterium to interact with host cells. Its metabolism and genetic variability also enable it to adapt to different conditions within animal and human hosts.

jejuni is primarily associated with contaminated food or water. The bacterium occurs worldwide, although its prevalence and transmission vary among populations and geographic regions. Although most infections resolve without prolonged illness, complications can occasionally occur, including development of Guillain, Barré syndrome and reactive arthritis.

body.text: History

Campylobacter jejuni was originally named Vibrio jejuni in 1931 due to its resemblance to other Vibrio species. In 1963, Sebald and Vérnon proposed the genus Campylobacter based on characteristics such as low levels of guanine and cytosine (G +C), non-fermentative metabolism, and microaerophilic growth requirements.

The first well documented outbreak of human Campylobacter infection occurred in 1938, when contaminated milk associated with diarrhea among approximately 355 inmates at two state institutions in Illinois. Although bacteria resembling Campylobacter had been observed in humans as early as 1886, the organisms were first successfully isolated from human stool samples in 1972.
Advances in laboratory cultivation techniques during the 1970s helped establish C. jejuni as an important cause of bacterial gastroenteritis.

The genus name Campylobacter means "curved rod", deriving from the Greek words kampylos (curved) and baktron (rod). The species name jejuni was first proposed due to the species' occurrence in infected lesions around the jejunum. Among the species within this genus, C.
jejuni is considered important because of its role in human gastrointestinal infections and its worldwide public health significance.
Metabolism

jejuni has limited ability to metabolize sugars and relies mainly on amino acids and organic compounds as sources of carbon and energy. Most strains lack key enzymes needed for conventional glycolysis, including glucokinase and 6-phosphofructokinase. Important nutrients include serine, aspartate, and glutamate, while some strains can also utilize asparagine and proline.
These nutrients may come from the host or from metabolic products produced by other microorganisms in the gut.

Amino acids taken up C. jejuni feed into central metabolic pathways, including the citric acid cycle, non-oxidative pentose phosphate pathway, gluconeogenesis, and fatty acid synthesis. Serine can be converted to pyruvate by the SdaA dehydratase, while aspartate and glutamate provide intermediates for the citric acid cycle.
These pathways supply energy and produce molecules needed for biosynthesis and growth.

When preferred nutrients are limited, C. jejuni can also use acetate and lactate as carbon sources. Lactate produced by other mircoorganisms in the intestinal tract can be converted to pyruvate and used in central metabolism, while acetate can be reused as an additional carbon source.

Energy production occurs through respiration. Oxygen serves as an important terminal electron acceptor under the low oxygen conditions preferred by C. The bacterium can also use alternative electron acceptors, including fumarate, nitrate, and certain sulfur- and nitrogen-containing compounds. This respiratory flexibility allows C. jejuni to generate energy under different conditions in the intestinal environment.
Genome

jejuni strain NCTC11168 was first published in 2000. The original genome analysis predicted 1,654 protein-coding genes and 54 stable RNA species, although later re-annotation revised the number of predicted coding sequences to 1,643.

The genome contains relatively few repeated or phage-associated sequences but includes several hypervariable sequences. Many of these regions occur in genes involved in the production or modification of surface structures, including capsule and lipooligosaccharide. Changes within these regions can alter gene expression and contribute to variation among C.
Natural genetic transformation

jejuni is naturally competent, meaning it can take up DNA from its environment and incorporate it into its genome through natural genetic transformation. The acquired DNA can be incorporated into the bacterial genome by homologous recombination, contributing to genetic variation within the species. This process can also transfer genes associated with antibiotic resistance.
Transfer of resistance genes has been reported to occur more frequently in biofilms than between planktonic cells (single cells that float in liquid media).

jejuni commonly colonizes the intestinal tracts of birds and mammals, often without causing disease in the animal host. Poultry is considered the major animal reservoir of C. jejuni, with chickens and other poultry frequently carrying the bacterium in their gastrointestinal tract. jejuni is also found in cattle, sheep, dogs, cats, pigs, and several wildlife species.
Wild birds can carry genetically diverse strains of C. jejuni and may contribute to its circulation among wildlife, livestock, and surrounding environments.

jejuni can be detected in foods and environmental sources contaminated by animal waste. Poultry meat is an important food-associated source, while raw milk, untreated water, and contaminated produce can also contain the bacterium. Its presence in these sources generally reflects contamination originating from colonized animals or their feces.
Transmission

jejuni is primarily transmitted to humans by the fecal-oral route. Infection most often occurs after consuming contaminated food or water, especially undercooked poultry. Transmission can also occur through unpasteurized milk, contaminated produce, untreated water, or direct contact with infected animals.
Cross-contamination during food preparation can spread the bacterium from raw poultry to other foods or kitchen surfaces.
Virulence Factors
Flagella

Flagella are an important virulence factor of C. jejuni that enable motility, biofilm formation, host cell interactions and intestinal colonization in C. They also aid in the secretion of proteins involved in infection. Producing flagella requires high energy, so the bacterium must regulate their production.

CsrA is a post-transcriptional regulatory protein that binds flaA mRNA to inhibit its translation into FlaA, the major filament of the structure. Studies of csrA mutant strains have identified changes in proteins involved with motility, host cell interactions, stress resistance, and metabolism.
Chemotaxis

jejuni uses chemotaxis to adjust its movement in response to chemical gradients in its environment. It can move toward chemical attractants and away from repellents, helping it respond to favorable and unfavorable conditions.
Other virulence factors

The pgl locus enables C. jejuni to attach sugar groups and proteins through a process called N-linked glycosylation. This modification affects proteins involved in bacterial functions, including host adherence and invasion. jejuni secretes Campylobacter invasive antigens (Cia), which facilitate invasion.

The bacteria also produce cytolethal distending toxins (CDT), which damage host cell DNA and can disrupt the cell cycle, leading to cell enlargement, cell cycle arrest, and sometimes apoptosis. The lipopolysaccharide (LPS) of C. jejuni also contributes to virulence by stimulating host inflammatory response.
Pathogenesis
jejuni causes disease by moving through the intestinal environment, attaching to intestinal cells, sometimes entering those cells, producing toxins, and triggering inflammation and immune response.
Adherence and invasion

jejuni uses strategies to attach to and breach the intestinal epithelial layer of its host cells. It uses proteases, particularly HtrA, to disrupt cell junctions and cross the epithelial barrier. Host proteins such as fibronectin can serve as binding sites for C. jejuni and facilitate this process. After entering a host cell, C.

jejuni can survive inside membrane bound compartments called Campylobacter-containing vacuoles. Host cell transport mechanisms, including dynein, can help move these compartments toward the perinuclear region to avoid lysosomal degradation for up to 72 hours.
Toxins and inflammatory mechanisms

jejuni causes intestinal disease through interactions with gut enterocytes, production of bacterial toxins, and the host's inflammatory response. The best-characterized toxin produced by C. jejuni is cytolethal distending toxin (CDT). Although other toxin-like activities have been investigated, the contribution of individual secreted proteins to the development and severity of human disease is not fully understood.

jejuni's lipopolysaccharide (LPS), particularly its lipid A component, can influence how the immune system responds to the bacterium. Lipid A contains fatty acid chains that help determine how strongly the immune system is activated. One study found that LPS from a C.

jejuni strain containing a mixture of lipid A forms caused a moderate inflammatory response in mouse macrophages. coli LPS, it triggered lower levels of inflammatory cytokines. These findings suggest that differences in lipid A structure can influence the strength of immune response, although further research is needed to determine how these findings apply to humans.
